...First measurable lowland snow of the season tonight into Sunday...

Tonight through Sunday night: A low pressure system spinning at 
roughly 48N 135W in the eastern Pacific off of Vancouver Island
will push across an occluded frontal band tonight into Sunday. 
Precipitation will primarily be focused over the Cascades this 
evening where easterly flow at lower levels will also result in 
favorable orographics in additional to weak dynamics along the 
front and aloft. Temperatures this afternoon are running in the
low to mid 30s for much of this area and dew points around the 
the mid to upper 20s is expected to result in snow as the precip
type. How impactful the snow will be will be dependent on road 
temperatures and intensity of the snow. The prognoses is for a 
relatively light snow that is unlikely to overcome warmer road 
temperatures at the lowest elevations in the Wenatchee Area that
includes near the Wenatchee River at Cashmere and along the 
Columbia River. I expect that at least slushy accumulations will
occur further up the Wenatchee River and on the higher benches 
around Wenatchee and Chelan, as well as up the Methow Valley. 
Accumulating snow over the mountain passes and on the Waterville
Plateau is also expected where 1 to 3 inches of total snowfall 
is anticipated. Expect slippery travel overnight into Sunday 
morning with a Winter Weather Advisory in effect.

The frontal band will make it to the Spokane/Coeur d'Alene Area
and the Northeast Mountains to North Idaho later into Sunday 
morning into the afternoon. Valley locations, as well as 
Spokane/Cd'A are also expected to see snow, but a later start to
the snow with the intensity being light will make it more 
difficult for snow to accumulate on roads. This part of the 
forecast area may see appreciable snow accumulations mostly on 
grassy surfaces and on the shoulders of roads. Temperatures do 
look to cool down to below freezing for Sunday night and it may 
be after the snow stops with roads icing up that impacts are 
more likely to occur, and this may continue into the Monday 
commute period as well to start off the holiday week.

Monday through Wednesday: As preciously mentioned, Monday morning 
could start out a bit dicey for the commuting period with icy roads 
and walking surfaces. There is also indications for fog to develop 
behind the frontal band across the Columbia Basin into the the 
mountain valleys (include Spokane/Cd'A) as precip will moisten up 
the boundary layer and it won't take much cooling with a depreciated 
dew point depression for fog to form. A warm front skirts across the 
Cascades Tuesday into Tuesday night. Model guidance doesn't show as 
much moisture as previous forecasts with snow accumulations 
over Stevens Pass and Washington Pass decreasing down to around 
2 to 4 inches over this period. Those looking to travel across 
the Cascades before the Thanksgiving holiday should be mindful 
of road conditions over the Cascade passes on Tuesday. 
Snoqualmie will also see the potential for light snow.

Wednesday night through Saturday: Round out the latter half of the 
busy holiday travel period with concerns for impacts mainly just at 
the mountain passes. A weak Atmospheric River (AR) penetrates 
into the interior portions of the Northwest Region on 
Thanksgiving. The increased moisture will act to modify the air
mass with mainly rain and mountain snow expected. Snow levels 
will be tricky though as they will be hovering right around 
mountain pass level and could result in travel impacts for 
anyone looking to travel over Stevens Pass in the evening before
Thanksgiving with snow levels between 4000 to 4500 feet. 
Snoqualmie looks to see precip type as rain, but Stevens Pass 
may be a heavy wet snow. Snow levels also look to be near or 
above pass level for Lookout. Temperatures see a warming trend 
over the holiday week with highs expected to be in the 40s for 
Thanksgiving afternoon, but that also may come with rain with 
much of the region having a 60 percent chance or higher. Turkey 
trots in the morning could be on the wet side. Winds also look 
to be a breezy with gusts potentially up to 30-35 mph across the
exposed areas of the Columbia Basin for the afternoon on 
Thanksgiving day.

There is greater uncertainty with potential for precip after 
Thanksgiving. Model ensembles build up a ridge of higher 
pressure over the West. Some ensemble members takes energy over
the eastern Pacific and undercuts the ridge with additional 
light precipitation into the post Thanksgiving weekend. Other 
members weakens the shortwave energy more considerably with a 
mainly dry forecast except over the Cascades. The good news is 
that snow levels looks to continue to increase with rain over 
Stevens Pass and Lookout Pass. Only the lesser traveled 
Washington Pass and Sherman Pass to potentially see light snow. Check
back for forecast updates if your plans could be impacted by 
the active weather pattern. /SVH
